title: Does your entire body replace itself every seven years?
hook: Renewal follows several timetables: from days to decades, depending on the cells.
summary: There is no complete replacement every seven years: different cells have different lifespans, and some neurons persist for decades.
cardText: No. Stomach surface cells are replaced within days; red cells last about four months. Studies have found neurons approximately as old as the person. There is no synchronized whole-body replacement.

cardBlocks.text: The body does not exchange all its cells for a fresh set every seven years. Compare a few of its timetables: stomach surface cells are replaced within days, while red blood cells live about 120 days, roughly four months. Renewal does not follow one universal calendar.

Some neurons, or nerve cells, persist for decades. In a study of human brain tissue, scientists measured carbon-14 in DNA and found neurons approximately as old as the person. This contrasts with tissues that rapidly replace cells. Keeping old cells and producing new ones coexist in the same body, rather than happening as one synchronized exchange.
There is no complete seven-year exchange: cells from different tissues can last from days to decades.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Above-ground nuclear tests increased atmospheric carbon-14 during the Cold War. That signal, incorporated into DNA, allowed researchers to estimate when cells formed. The study compared DNA carbon-14 levels with atmospheric records.

The finding about old neurons does not mean adults never make new neurons. Researchers have also found neuron formation in the hippocampus, a region important for forming memories. These are different regions and cell populations: a result need not apply to the entire brain.
